chunks: Package-on-package chips and trade-offs. The question: What are package on package (PoP) chips? What are their tradeoffs?
Package-on-package, or PoP, stacks one chip package on top of another.
Usually a memory package sits on a processor package, joined by small solder balls, and the pair is soldered to the board as one part.
It saves board space and makes the connection between processor and memory very short. The costs are heat, extra height, and harder repair.
Think of two buildings that must work closely together. Side by side, they need two plots of land and a long walkway between them.
Stacked as one two-story building, they need one plot and a short staircase.
The catch is that the upper floor sits right above the furnace, so it gets warm and blocks one route the heat could take out.
The SoC die sits in the bottom package's cavity region, surrounded by a ring of interface balls (orange) that land the memory package above it.
The memory's own dies are wire-bonded inside the top package. The SoC die is directly under the memory, which is the source of the thermal coupling.
Package: the case around a chip, with the connections to the board. The stack is soldered like a ball grid array.
SoC (system on chip): one chip holding the processor and many other blocks. LPDDR: a low-power memory type used in phones. It is a wide, fast interface.
Flight time: how long a signal takes to travel from one chip to the other. Yield: the share of parts that work.
Signals travel about 6. 2 picoseconds (trillionths of a second) per millimeter on a circuit board. A memory route of 25 mm across the board takes about 156 picoseconds.
Inside a PoP stack the link is about 3 mm, so about 19 picoseconds. For a common LPDDR speed, one bit lasts about 234 picoseconds on the wire.
The board route uses about two thirds of that, and the stack link only about 8%. Stacking has a cost too.
If each package works 98% of the time and stacking works 99%, the stack works 0. 98 times 0. 98 times 0. 99 about 95% of the time, so makers test each package first.
That is the whole idea.
"Package-on-package stacks a memory package, usually LPDDR, on top of a processor package, joined by solder balls.
It saves board area and gives a very short, low-capacitance memory interface, so less delay and I/O power: 3 mm of stack versus about 25 mm of PCB trace is roughly 19 versus 156 picoseconds.
The downsides are thermal coupling since the DRAM sits on the hottest die, extra height, warpage at reflow, yield compounding when stacking, fixed memory after assembly and hard rework."
